decks.title: Market Mechanism — Part 1: Equilibrium and Changes in Demand and Supply
goals: Find the equilibrium price and quantity from schedules and from equations
Explain how excess demand and excess supply restore equilibrium
Show the effect of shifts in demand or in supply on equilibrium
Predict the outcome when demand and supply change together

slides.heading: Market Mechanism: Equilibrium Price
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how buyers and sellers settle on a **price**, and what happens when **demand** or **supply** changes.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: equilibrium, excess demand and supply, changes in demand, changes in supply, and both changing together
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the last chapters we studied buyers and sellers separately. Now we bring them together in one market. We will see how a price settles where buyers and sellers agree, why any other price does not last, and what happens to price and quantity when demand, supply or both of them change.

slides.heading: Where demand meets supply
slides.body_md: The **equilibrium price** is the price at which **quantity demanded = quantity supplied**. The quantity traded there is the **equilibrium quantity**.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined jaggery market in a Kolhapur mandi. The demand curve slopes down and the supply curve slopes up. They cross at one point, marked E. At thirty rupees a kilogram, buyers want sixty tonnes a week and sellers offer exactly sixty tonnes. That price clears the market, so it is the equilibrium price.

slides.narration: The schedule tells the same story in numbers. At twenty and twenty-five rupees, buyers want more than sellers offer. At thirty-five and forty rupees, sellers offer more than buyers want. Only at thirty rupees do the two columns match. Always look for the row where demand equals supply.

slides.heading: Excess demand and excess supply
slides.body_md: Below E the market has **excess demand**; above E it has **excess supply**.

visual.alt: The jaggery demand and supply curves with two horizontal gaps: at 20 rupees buyers want 80 tonnes but sellers offer 30, an excess demand of 50; at 40 rupees sellers offer 90 but buyers want 40, an excess supply of 50; both gaps close at E
visual.caption: Below E the price is pushed up; above E it is pushed down.

slides.narration: At twenty rupees buyers want eighty tonnes but only thirty are offered: an excess demand of fifty. At forty rupees sellers bring ninety tonnes but buyers take only forty: an excess supply of fifty. Neither situation can last, because someone in the market is left unsatisfied.

slides.heading: How the market corrects itself
bullets: Excess demand: buyers compete, the price **rises**.
Excess supply: sellers cut the price, the price **falls**.
Along the way buyers and sellers **move along** their curves; no curve shifts.

nodes.label: Price rises: demand contracts, supply extends

visual.alt: Flow of price adjustment: a price below equilibrium creates excess demand, buyers compete, the price rises so demand contracts and supply extends, and the gap closes at equilibrium
visual.caption: The same logic runs in reverse above E

slides.narration: When buyers cannot get enough at the ruling price, they offer more, and the price rises. As it rises, buyers ask for less and sellers offer more, until the gap disappears. With unsold stock the opposite happens. Notice that nothing shifts here: everyone simply moves along their own curve back to equilibrium.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: solving for equilibrium
slides.body_md: An imagined Ratnagiri mango-pulp cooperative: **Qd = 90 − 3P** and **Qs = 2P − 10**.

visual.alt: Worked example table solving the imagined Ratnagiri mango-pulp market: setting 90 minus 3P equal to 2P minus 10 gives a price of 20 rupees and a quantity of 30 tonnes, checked with the supply equation

slides.narration: To find equilibrium from equations, set demand equal to supply. Ninety minus three P equals two P minus ten, so five P equals one hundred and the price is twenty rupees. Put it back into the demand equation to get thirty tonnes, and check that the supply equation gives the same thirty.

slides.narration: Suppose festival buying raises the demand for jaggery at every price. The demand curve shifts right, and at the old price there is excess demand. The price rises to thirty-five rupees and seventy-five tonnes change hands. A health campaign that lowers demand does the reverse: twenty-five rupees and forty-five tonnes.

slides.narration: New storage sheds raise the supply of jaggery at every price. The supply curve shifts right, the price falls to twenty-five rupees and the quantity rises to seventy tonnes. Unseasonal rain that cuts supply pushes the price up to thirty-five rupees and the quantity down to fifty tonnes.

slides.heading: Four single shifts at a glance

visual.alt: Table of single shifts: a demand increase raises price and quantity; a demand decrease lowers both; a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity; a supply decrease raises price and lowers quantity

slides.narration: Here are the four cases side by side. A demand shift moves price and quantity in the same direction. A supply shift moves them in opposite directions. Learn this pattern and you can answer most one-mark questions on this topic quickly and correctly.

slides.heading: When both curves shift
slides.body_md: If both shift the **same way**, the change in **quantity** is certain; if they shift **opposite ways**, the change in **price** is certain.

visual.alt: Table of simultaneous shifts: when demand and supply move in the same direction quantity is certain and price depends on the sizes of the shifts; when they move in opposite directions price is certain and quantity depends on the sizes
visual.caption: Equal shifts in the same direction leave the price unchanged.

slides.narration: When demand and supply both increase, quantity certainly rises, but the price depends on which shift is bigger. When demand rises while supply falls, the price certainly rises, but quantity depends on the sizes of the two shifts. Always say what is certain and what depends on the sizes.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: equal shifts
slides.body_md: Demand rises to **Qd = 145 − 2P** and supply to **Qs = 3P − 5**: each by 25 tonnes at every price.

visual.alt: Worked example table: when demand and supply both rise by 25 tonnes at every price, the jaggery price stays at 30 rupees and the quantity rises from 60 to 85 tonnes

slides.narration: Solving the new pair gives a price of thirty rupees, exactly the old price, and eighty-five tonnes. Because both curves moved right by the same twenty-five tonnes, the extra demand and the extra supply cancel at the old price. So the price does not change, but the quantity rises by twenty-five tonnes.

slides.heading: Equal shifts on a diagram

visual.alt: Demand and supply both shift right by the same amount. The old equilibrium E at 60 tonnes and the new equilibrium E1 at 85 tonnes lie on the same horizontal line at 30 rupees, so the price is unchanged while the quantity rises
visual.caption: Equal shifts: Qd = 145 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 5 meet at the old price.

slides.narration: The diagram confirms it. The old and new intersections lie on the same horizontal line at thirty rupees. The new point is further right, showing the larger quantity traded. Draw both old curves dashed and both new curves solid so the examiner can follow your answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: equal increases
slides.body_md: Choose the correct effect on the shirt market.
slides.narration: Ask whether any excess appears at the old price when both curves move by the same amount.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Excess demand pushes the price up
Excess supply pushes the price down
Demand moves price and quantity together; supply moves them apart
Same direction: quantity certain; opposite: price certain

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: equilibrium, excess demand and supply, single shifts and simultaneous shifts

slides.narration: To sum up: equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Below it, excess demand pushes the price up; above it, excess supply pushes it down. A shift in demand moves price and quantity together, a shift in supply moves them apart, and when both shift, one result is certain and the other depends on sizes.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Label axes (quantity across, price up), curves (DD, SS) and points (E, E1).
For shifts, draw the old curve, the new curve and both equilibria.
With equations, solve the new pair: do not just add the shift to the old quantity.
For simultaneous changes, state what is certain and what depends on sizes.
2 marks: two points or a labelled diagram; 3 marks: working plus comment; 5 marks: parts in order.
slides.narration: Examiners reward clear diagrams. Label both axes, both curves and every equilibrium point. When a curve shifts, keep the old one so the change is visible. When solving equations, always solve the new pair. And for two shifts at once, say which result is certain and which depends on the sizes of the shifts.

goals: Explain why a price ceiling below equilibrium causes a shortage, rationing and black markets
Explain why a price floor above equilibrium causes a surplus, using minimum support prices
Calculate shortages and surpluses from demand and supply equations
Weigh the gains and costs of price controls

slides.heading: When the Government Fixes Prices
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **price ceilings** and **price floors**, and the **minimum support price** for crops.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why control prices, price ceilings, rationing and black markets, price floors and minimum support prices, gains and costs
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Sometimes the market price is thought to be unfair, either too high for poor buyers or too low for farmers. Then the government may fix a price by law. In this part we see what happens to a market when a maximum or a minimum price is fixed, and why such controls need extra measures to work.

slides.heading: Two kinds of price control

rows: Atta in a cut-off hill district

visual.alt: Two-row table: a price ceiling is a maximum set below equilibrium to protect consumers, a price floor is a minimum set above equilibrium to protect producers, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: A price ceiling is a legal maximum. It matters only when it is below the equilibrium price and is meant to protect consumers. A price floor is a legal minimum. It matters only when it is above equilibrium and is meant to protect producers. Our examples are imagined, but the logic applies everywhere.

slides.heading: A ceiling creates a shortage
slides.body_md: At a ceiling **below E**, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

slides.narration: Road blockages cut the supply of atta in an imagined hill district, and the state caps the price at twenty-five rupees, below the market-clearing thirty. slides.narration: First find the free-market equilibrium: thirty rupees and eighty tonnes. Then put the ceiling price into both equations. slides.narration: Think about buyers who cannot get the good at the legal price but are willing to pay more.

slides.heading: Rationing and black markets
bullets: **Rationing:** the limited supply is shared by quota, for example through ration cards.
**Black market:** some stock is sold secretly above the legal price.
Neither removes the shortage; only more supply or a higher price can.

nodes.label: Black market above the legal price

visual.alt: Flow of the effects of a price ceiling: a ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, which leads to queues and rationing, and to black-market sales above the legal price
visual.caption: Why a ceiling needs rationing

slides.narration: Because buyers want more than is available, the government shares the limited quantity by quota, often with ration cards and fair-price shops. Some buyers who miss out pay more in secret, so a black market appears. These measures share the shortage, but they do not end it; only more supply would.

slides.heading: How the minimum support price works
slides.body_md: For notified crops, the **Government of India** announces MSPs on the recommendation of the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**.

visual.alt: Flow of the minimum support price system: the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices recommends, the Government of India announces the support price, agencies buy at that price, grain is stored as buffer stock and used for ration shops and reserves

slides.narration: In India, the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices recommends support prices for notified crops, and the Government of India announces them. sections.heading: 1. Market equilibrium
sections.body_md:
**Equilibrium** is the price at which **quantity demanded equals quantity supplied**. It clears the market: no unsold stock and no unmet demand.

From equations Qd = a − bP and Qs = c + dP, set a − bP = c + dP and solve for P, then find Q. Example (imagined Kolhapur jaggery): 120 − 2P = 3P − 30 gives **₹30** and **60 t**.

key_terms.definition_md: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
No surplus and no shortage at the ruling price.

sections.heading: 2. Excess demand and excess supply
sections.body_md:
- **Excess demand** (price below E): buyers compete, the price **rises**; demand contracts and supply extends. At ₹20: 80 − 30 = **50 t**.
- **Excess supply** (price above E): sellers cut the price, which **falls**; demand extends and supply contracts. At ₹40: 90 − 40 = **50 t**.

During this adjustment no curve shifts: buyers and sellers move along their curves.

key_terms.definition_md: Quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium.
Quantity supplied minus quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium.

sections.heading: 3. Changes in demand or in supply
sections.body_md:
- **Demand increases:** price and quantity both rise. **Demand decreases:** both fall.
- **Supply increases:** price falls, quantity rises. **Supply decreases:** price rises, quantity falls.

To calculate, solve the **new pair of equations**; the change in quantity is smaller than the shift because the price also changes.

sections.heading: 4. Simultaneous changes
sections.body_md:
- **Same direction:** quantity is certain (rises if both increase); price depends on which shift is larger; **equal shifts leave the price unchanged**.
- **Opposite directions:** price is certain (rises if demand rises and supply falls); quantity depends on the relative shifts.

sections.heading: 5. Price ceiling, rationing and black markets
sections.body_md:
A **price ceiling** is a legal **maximum** set **below** equilibrium to protect consumers. It creates a **shortage** (Qd > Qs). The government shares the supply by **rationing** (ration cards, fair-price shops), and some sellers sell secretly above the limit in a **black market**.

Imagined atta: at ₹25, Qd = 100 and Qs = 50, a shortage of **50 t**.

key_terms.definition_md: A legal maximum price below equilibrium.
Sharing a scarce good by quota rather than by price.
Illegal sale of a controlled good above its legal price.

sections.heading: 6. Price floor and minimum support price
sections.body_md:
A **price floor** is a legal **minimum** set **above** equilibrium to protect producers. It creates a **surplus** (Qs > Qd). In India, **minimum support prices** for notified crops are announced by the **Government of India** on the recommendation of the **CACP**; public agencies buy the surplus and hold it as **buffer stock**, part of which goes to ration shops.

Imagined lentils: at 70, Qs = 250 and Qd = 150, a surplus of **100** thousand quintals.

key_terms.definition_md: A legal minimum price above equilibrium.
The price at which the government stands ready to buy a notified crop.
Grain held by the government to steady supplies and prices.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Placing a ceiling above equilibrium (it would have no effect) or a floor below it.
- Saying excess demand shifts the demand curve: the adjustment is a movement along both curves.
- Adding a shift to the old quantity instead of solving the new pair of equations.
- Claiming a definite price change when both curves move the same way by unknown amounts.
- Saying rationing removes a shortage: it only shares it.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: the correct option or a one-line answer.
- 2 marks: two points, or a labelled diagram with one point.
- 3 marks: working with the answer and a comment.
- 5 marks: each part answered in order with diagrams.
- Board papers also set 4-mark (2 + 2) and 8-mark (4 + 4) questions in parts.

questions.stem_md: In a competitive market, the equilibrium price of a commodity is the price at which

options.text_md: sellers earn the highest possible profit
the quantity buyers wish to buy equals the quantity sellers wish to sell
the government says the good should be sold
buyers spend the largest possible amount on the good

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the quantity buyers wish to buy equals the quantity sellers wish to sell. Equilibrium means market demand equals market supply, so there is no pressure on the price to change. Profit, government decisions and total spending do not define it.

questions.stem_md: A weekly schedule for jaggery in an imagined Kolhapur mandi reads: at ₹25 a kg, 70 tonnes demanded and 45 supplied; at ₹30, 60 and 60; at ₹35, 50 and 75. The equilibrium price and quantity are

options.text_md: ₹25 and 70 tonnes
₹35 and 75 tonnes
₹30 and 120 tonnes
₹30 and 60 tonnes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹30 and 60 tonnes. Only at ₹30 is the quantity demanded (60) equal to the quantity supplied (60). At ₹25 demand exceeds supply; at ₹35 supply exceeds demand; and equilibrium quantity is not the sum of both sides.

questions.stem_md: At a price below equilibrium in the market for school notebooks in an imagined Patna bazaar, which situation arises, and how does the price respond?

options.text_md: Excess demand arises and competition among buyers pushes the price up
Excess supply arises and sellers cut the price
Excess demand arises and the price falls further
The market is in equilibrium, so the price does not change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Excess demand arises and competition among buyers pushes the price up. Below equilibrium more is demanded than supplied: excess demand. Unsatisfied buyers bid the price up until demand and supply match again.

options.text_md: the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
the Reserve Bank of India
the Competition Commission of India
each district collector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP). The CACP recommends MSPs for notified crops, and the Government of India announces them.

questions.stem_md: When a support price leaves farmers with grain that the market will not buy, what does the government usually do with the surplus it procures?

options.text_md: Burns it to keep prices high
Exports all of it at a loss every year
Returns it to farmers after paying them
Holds it as buffer stock and distributes some through ration shops

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Holds it as buffer stock and distributes some through ration shops. Procured grain is stored as buffer stock and used for the public distribution system and to calm prices in bad years. The other options are not the usual use.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A minimum support price fixed above the equilibrium price creates a surplus of the crop.

**Reason (R):** At a price above equilibrium, farmers grow less and buyers want more.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: above equilibrium, farmers offer **more** (supply extends) and buyers want **less** (demand contracts), which is why a surplus appears.

questions.stem_md: True or false? To keep a support price effective, the government must stand ready to buy the surplus that the market does not take at that price.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Without procurement, unsold stock would push the market price below the support level; buying the surplus keeps the floor in force.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined lentil market, demand is Qd = 500 − 5P (P in ₹ hundred per quintal). How much will private buyers purchase at the support price of 70?
questions.solution_md: Qd = 500 − 5 × 70 = 150 thousand quintals.

questions.stem_md: Give two aims of announcing minimum support prices for crops such as wheat and paddy.
questions.solution_md: Two aims of MSP.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To **protect farmers' incomes** from a sharp fall in prices after a good harvest.
2. To **encourage production** of crops the country needs and to build **buffer stocks** for food security.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with a described diagram, the effect of a support price fixed above the equilibrium price of maize in an imagined Bihar district.
questions.solution_md: Diagram with the surplus, then procurement.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw DD and SS meeting at E (P*, Q*). A horizontal line at the **floor Pf above P*** meets DD at Qd and SS at Qs, with **Qs greater than Qd**: the gap is a **surplus**.
Farmers grow more and buyers buy less; to keep the floor, the government **procures the surplus** and stores it as **buffer stock**.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined lentil market (Qd = 500 − 5P, Qs = 5P − 100), the support price is 70. Find the surplus and give one benefit and one cost of this policy.
questions.solution_md: Surplus calculation, then one benefit and one cost.

answer.model_answer_md:
At 70: Qs = **250**, Qd = **150**, so the **surplus is 100 thousand quintals**, which the government must buy.
**Benefit:** farmers get an assured, higher income.
**Cost:** public money is spent on buying and **storing** the surplus, and consumers pay more than the free-market price of 60.

questions.stem_md: For lentils in an imagined Madhya Pradesh district (Qd = 500 − 5P, Qs = 5P − 100; P in ₹ hundred per quintal, Q in thousand quintals): (a) find the free-market equilibrium [1]; (b) find the surplus at a support price of 70 and explain it with a described diagram [3]; (c) evaluate whether such a support price helps the economy [1].
questions.solution_md: Equilibrium, surplus with diagram, balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 500 − 5P = 5P − 100 gives **P = 60**, **Q = 200** thousand quintals.
(b) At 70: Qs = 250, Qd = 150, **surplus 100**. In the diagram the floor line lies above E; supply extends to Qs and demand contracts to Qd, and the gap is bought by the government as **buffer stock**.
(c) It **protects farmers** and builds food reserves, but it **costs public money** for procurement and storage and can encourage over-production of one crop; it helps most when used with care.

questions.stem_md: Compare a price ceiling and a price floor under these heads, with an imagined Indian example of each: (a) position relative to equilibrium; (b) market result; (c) government action needed to support it; (d) who gains; (e) one problem it may cause.
questions.solution_md: Five contrasts with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Position:** a **ceiling** is a legal maximum set **below** the equilibrium price; a **floor** is a legal minimum set **above** it. On the wrong side of equilibrium either control has no effect.
(b) **Result:** a ceiling makes quantity demanded exceed quantity supplied, a **shortage**; a floor makes quantity supplied exceed quantity demanded, a **surplus**.
(c) **Support needed:** a ceiling needs **rationing** of the limited supply; a floor needs government **procurement** of the unsold surplus.
(d) **Who gains:** a ceiling helps **consumers**, for example poor households buying kerosene in an imagined district; a floor helps **producers**, for example wheat farmers receiving a support price.
(e) **Problem:** a ceiling can lead to **black markets**; a floor can lead to **storage costs and wastage** of procured grain.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about saffron in an imagined Pampore market. [2 + 2]

(i) Early snowfall damages the crop, while a wedding season raises demand. With a described diagram, explain the certain effect on the price of saffron.
(ii) A trader says the quantity of saffron sold "must fall". Is the trader right? Justify.
questions.solution_md: Certain price rise; uncertain quantity.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Supply shifts **left** and demand shifts **right**. Both create **excess demand** at the old price, so the **price certainly rises**; in the diagram E₁ lies above E.
(ii) **Not necessarily.** The fall in supply reduces quantity but the rise in demand increases it, so quantity **falls only if the supply shift is larger**; it could rise or stay the same.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) An imagined state caps the price of refill cylinders for a small cooking stove below the market-clearing level. Explain the immediate effect on the market with a described diagram.
(ii) A year later the cap is removed. Explain how the market moves back to equilibrium.
questions.solution_md: Shortage under the cap; upward adjustment after removal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) At the cap, **quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied**: a **shortage**, shown as the gap between DD and SS along the cap line below E. Queues, rationing or black-market sales follow.
(ii) Without the cap, unsatisfied buyers **bid the price up**; demand **contracts** and supply **extends** until the price reaches the **equilibrium**, where the shortage disappears.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) movements along both curves to E

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined Kolhapur jaggery mandi, where Qd = 120 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 30 (P in ₹ per kg, Q in tonnes a week). [4 + 4]

(i) Find the equilibrium and explain, with figures, the excess demand at ₹20 and the excess supply at ₹40.
(ii) Demand later rises to Qd = 145 − 2P while new storage raises supply to Qs = 3P − 5. Find the new equilibrium and explain why the price does not change.
questions.solution_md: Equilibrium and disequilibria, then equal shifts.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Setting demand equal to supply, 120 − 2P = 3P − 30, so 5P = 150. The equilibrium is **₹30 a kg** and **60 tonnes** a week, where the two curves cross at E.
At ₹20, buyers want 80 t but sellers offer only 30 t: an **excess demand of 50 t**. Buyers who cannot get jaggery offer more, so the price **rises**; demand contracts and supply extends.
At ₹40, sellers offer 90 t but buyers want only 40 t: an **excess supply of 50 t**. Sellers with unsold stock cut the price, so it **falls**; demand extends and supply contracts. In both cases the market returns to E without any curve shifting.
(ii) The new pair 145 − 2P = 3P − 5 gives 5P = 150, so the price is **₹30** and the quantity **85 t**. Each curve moved right by **25 tonnes at every price**. At the old price of ₹30, buyers now want 25 t more and sellers offer 25 t more, so no excess demand or excess supply arises. With no pressure on the price, it **stays at ₹30**, while the quantity traded **rises by 25 t**.

marking_scheme.step: Equal shifts at the old price

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) For atta in an imagined hill district (Qd = 200 − 4P, Qs = 6P − 100), calculate the shortage at a ceiling of ₹25 and explain two consequences of the ceiling.
(ii) For lentils in an imagined district (Qd = 500 − 5P, Qs = 5P − 100), calculate the surplus at a support price of 70 and evaluate the support price as a policy.
questions.solution_md: Shortage and two consequences; surplus and a balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) At the ceiling of ₹25, quantity demanded is 200 − 100 = **100 t** and quantity supplied is 150 − 100 = **50 t**, so there is a **shortage of 50 t** a week (the free market would clear at ₹30 and 80 t).
**Consequence 1 — rationing:** because buyers want twice what is available, the administration shares the 50 t through **ration cards and fair-price shops**, so each family gets a fixed quota.
**Consequence 2 — black market:** families left without atta are willing to pay more, so some sellers divert stock and sell it secretly **above ₹25**.
(ii) At the support price of 70, quantity supplied is **250** and quantity demanded is **150**, so there is a **surplus of 100** thousand quintals, which public agencies must buy and hold as **buffer stock**.
**Evaluation:** the policy **protects farm incomes** from price crashes and builds **food reserves** for lean years and ration shops. But it **costs public money** for procurement and storage, risks **wastage**, and makes consumers pay more than the free-market price of 60. On balance it is useful when it is targeted at needy farmers and the stocks are well managed.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined market report from a Lasalgaon-like onion yard and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined yard, traders and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Settled price with no unsold stock.

**(b)** Reduced arrivals mean a decrease in supply.

**(c) (i)** Supply increase, excess supply, falling price, extension of demand.

**OR (c) (ii)** Opposite supply shifts with opposite price effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The price **settled at ₹22** and **all stocks were sold**, so quantity demanded equalled quantity supplied.

**(b)** The **supply curve shifted left**: fewer onions reached the yard at every price.

**(c) (i)** The bumper harvest **shifted supply right**, so at the high Wednesday price there was **excess supply** (unsold heaps). Traders **cut rates**; buyers moved down their unchanged demand curve and bought more, until a new, lower equilibrium price was reached.

**OR (c) (ii)** Wednesday: a **decrease in supply** raised the **price** and lowered the **quantity** traded. Friday: an **increase in supply** lowered the **price** and raised the **quantity**. In both cases demand was unchanged, so only supply moved.

questions.passage_md:
**Weekly onion report, Godavari Valley yard (imagined)**

Monday: Arrivals were normal and the price settled at ₹22 a kg, with all stocks sold. Wednesday: Heavy rain upstream stopped trucks from three villages; arrivals fell sharply and the price climbed. Friday: Rain stopped and a bumper harvest from new fields arrived. Traders found unsold heaps at the earlier high price and began cutting rates. Buyers from city markets, whose demand did not change through the week, bought more as rates fell.

children.solution_md: Settled price with no unsold stock.

answer.model_answer_md: The price **settled at ₹22** and **all stocks were sold**, so quantity demanded equalled quantity supplied.

children.stem_md: Which curve shifted on Wednesday, and in which direction?
children.solution_md: Reduced arrivals mean a decrease in supply.

answer.model_answer_md: The **supply curve shifted left**: fewer onions reached the yard at every price.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain the Friday events using excess supply and the movement towards a new equilibrium.
children.solution_md: Supply increase, excess supply, falling price, extension of demand.

answer.model_answer_md: The bumper harvest **shifted supply right**, so at the high Wednesday price there was **excess supply** (unsold heaps). Traders **cut rates**; buyers moved down their unchanged demand curve and bought more, until a new, lower equilibrium price was reached.

Price falls to a new equilibrium; demand extends

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Compare the Wednesday and Friday changes in the yard and their effects on the price and quantity of onions.
alternatives.solution_md: Opposite supply shifts with opposite price effects.

answer.model_answer_md: Wednesday: a **decrease in supply** raised the **price** and lowered the **quantity** traded. Friday: an **increase in supply** lowered the **price** and raised the **quantity**. In both cases demand was unchanged, so only supply moved.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined extract from a district food officer's notes in a hill district and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the district and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Qd = 200 − 100 = 100; Qs = 150 − 100 = 50; shortage = 100 − 50 = 50 tonnes.

**(b)** Illegal sale above the cap.

**(c) (i)** Use buffer stock to raise supply.

**OR (c) (ii)** Floor creates surplus, procured as buffer stock.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **50 tonnes**

**(b)** A **black market**: the controlled good is sold illegally above the ceiling price.

**(c) (i)** Releasing the procured wheat (as atta) through **ration shops** adds to supply in the district, **shifting supply right**; the gap between demand and supply at ₹25 narrows, so queues and black-market sales fall.

**OR (c) (ii)** Wheat bought at a **support price above equilibrium** created a **surplus** in the plains; the government **procured** it and holds it as **buffer stock**, which can now be used in shortages.

questions.passage_md:
**Notes of the district food officer (imagined), monsoon season**

Road blockages cut the supply of atta. In the open market, demand is Qd = 200 − 4P and supply Qs = 6P − 100 (P in ₹ per kg, Q in tonnes a week). The state has capped the price at ₹25 a kg. Long queues have formed at shops, and there are reports of atta being sold at ₹40 a kg in back lanes. Meanwhile, wheat procured at the support price from the plains is lying in central godowns.

Name the problem described by "sold at ₹40 a kg in back lanes".

answer.model_answer_md: A **black market**: the controlled good is sold illegally above the ceiling price.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Suggest how the stock in the godowns could reduce the shortage, and explain its effect on the market.

answer.model_answer_md: Releasing the procured wheat (as atta) through **ration shops** adds to supply in the district, **shifting supply right**; the gap between demand and supply at ₹25 narrows, so queues and black-market sales fall.
